disease.inheritance: Autosomal dominant (activating KCNJ11 mutations); can be de novo
disease.mechanism: Gain-of-function ion channel. Activating KCNJ11 mutations prevent the ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel from closing, keeping the pancreatic beta-cell hyperpolarized and suppressing insulin secretion. This causes neonatal diabetes. The toxic species is a hyperactive channel, NOT an accumulating protein.
disease.recommended_modality: channel_blocker (sulfonylurea — closes the KATP channel, restoring insulin secretion)
disease.autotac_rationale: NOT eligible. The disease is a gain-of-function ION CHANNEL, not a toxic aggregate. The correct modality is a channel BLOCKER (sulfonylurea) that closes the hyperactive KATP channel and restores insulin secretion — not protein degradation.
disease.prevalence: ~1 in 100,000-260,000 live births — commonly cited; UNVERIFIED exact figure this session
disease.age_of_onset: First 6 months of life (hyperglycemia, failure to thrive)

approved_treatments.mechanism_correct: Sulfonylureas bind and close the KATP channel, depolarizing the beta-cell and restoring insulin secretion. Most patients with KCNJ11 neonatal diabetes can be switched from insulin to oral sulfonylureas, often with better glycemic control.
approved_treatments.fda_approval: Long-established (off-label for neonatal diabetes; NEJM 2006 demonstrated the switch)
approved_treatments.note: MW 494.0 Da, CID 3488 (glibenclamide) — commonly cited. This is a channel-blocker strategy, fundamentally different from degrader/replacement.

investigational: No degrader or gene therapy indicated — the channel blocker is the definitive approach

references.accession: Switching from Insulin to Oral Sulfonylureas (Pearson et al., NEJM 355:467)

disease.human_summary: Permanent neonatal diabetes due to KCNJ11 mutations is a gain-of-function channelopathy: an overactive ATP-sensitive potassium channel suppresses insulin secretion. The striking clinical result is that most patients can be switched from insulin injections to oral sulfonylurea tablets, which close the channel and restore insulin — a channel-blocker cure, not a degrader or replacement.
